domain.name: Distributed Systems
domain.description: High-availability replication, event loops, quorum consensus, and horizontal database sharding.

domainCoverage.synopsis: In distributed systems, networks are asynchronous, packet loss is normal, and clocks drift. This volume establishes the mental models from node replication and quorum to fault isolation.

chapters.title: TCP/IP & Linux Socket Networking Internals
chapters.summary: TCP delivers an in-order, guaranteed byte stream across unreliable packet-switched IP networks. The Linux kernel manages this via send/receive socket buffers (SO_SNDBUF/SO_RCVBUF), sliding-window flow control to protect receivers from saturation, and congestion algorithms (CUBIC/BBR) to regulate transmission across shared bottlenecks.

chapters.title: Reverse Proxy Patterns & Edge Load Balancing
chapters.summary: A reverse proxy acts as an intermediary gateway positioned between external clients and private backend services. It terminates client TLS handshakes, multiplexes requests across persistent upstream connection pools, distributes traffic via balancing algorithms (Round Robin, Least Connections, P2C), and guards internal services against direct internet exposure.

chapters.title: Load Balancing & Consistent Hashing
chapters.summary: Load balancing is the architectural discipline of distributing incoming network and application traffic across a pool of healthy backend servers to ensure high availability, prevent server saturation, and eliminate single points of failure. By decoupling client entry points from backend execution nodes, load balancers allow systems to scale horizontally from tens of requests to millions of requests per second.

chapters.title: CAP Theorem & PACELC
chapters.summary: The CAP Theorem (Brewer, 2000) proves that a distributed data store can guarantee at most two of three properties simultaneously: Consistency, Availability, and Partition Tolerance. Because physical networks inevitably experience packet drops, cable cuts, and latency spikes, Partition Tolerance (P) is unavoidable. Systems must deliberately choose CP (refusing stale writes/reads during network splits) or AP (serving stale data to keep uptime). PACELC extends this model to normal non-partitioned operation.

chapters.title: Consistent Hashing
chapters.summary: In distributed caching and storage, traditional modulo routing `hash(key) % N` remaps nearly 100% of keys whenever a server crashes or joins, triggering catastrophic cache stampedes. Consistent Hashing maps both data keys and server nodes onto the same virtual 32-bit ring ($0$ to $2^{32}-1$). Adding or removing a node only migrates $1/N$ of the keys, bounding rebalancing overhead and shielding database origins.

chapters.title: In-Memory Caching & Event Loop Architecture
chapters.summary: Caching is the architectural technique of retaining copies of frequently accessed, computationally expensive data in high-speed, volatile memory (e.g. Redis, Memcached, CPU caches) to bypass slow disk I/O, database table scans, and network hops. Proper caching slashes latency from tens of milliseconds to sub-milliseconds and shields databases from query saturation.

chapters.summary: The outbox table stores events in the same DB transaction as business rows; a relay process publishes to Kafka/RabbitMQ with at-least-once delivery.

chapters.title: Circuit Breakers & Resilience Patterns
chapters.summary: A circuit breaker wraps remote network calls in a stateful monitoring harness that automatically trips OPEN to fail-fast when downstream error or timeout thresholds breach, preventing caller thread exhaustion and cascading distributed outages. By failing fast, circuit breakers insulate upstream services and grant recovering dependencies breathing room to heal.

chapters.title: Bulkhead & Fault Isolation
chapters.summary: The bulkhead pattern limits resources per dependency or tenant—like ship compartments—so failures stay localized.

chapters.title: Rate Limiting Algorithms & Token Buckets
chapters.summary: Rate limiting controls the consumption rate of system resources by restricting the number of API calls or operations a client can make within a specified window. Proper rate limiting prevents denial-of-service (DoS) attacks, isolates noisy tenants in multi-tenant architectures, smooths burst traffic, and enforces commercial usage quotas.

theory.overview: Distributed computing begins at the physical network boundary. Unlike single-machine architectures with shared memory and nanosecond bus latencies, distributed nodes communicate across unbonded physical networks where packets are subject to unbounded delay, packet reordering, jitter, and arbitrary drops. Understanding transport mechanics, edge reverse proxies, and latency hierarchies establishes the physical baseline for all distributed protocols.
theory.whyItMatters: Every distributed outage traces back to physical network and socket constraints. Without understanding network boundaries, higher-level abstractions like consensus and replication fail under load.
keyMechanisms: The 8 Fallacies of Distributed Computing: Networks are unreliable, latency is non-zero, and bandwidth is finite.
TCP Transport Mechanics: 3-way handshake, sliding window flow control, congestion avoidance, and head-of-line blocking.
Reverse Proxy & Edge Ingress: TLS termination, HTTP/2 multiplexing, connection pooling, and backend origin protection.
Latency Hierarchy: CPU L1 (1ns) vs RAM (100ns) vs Intra-DC (0.5ms) vs Cross-Continent (100ms).

theory.overview: Time in distributed systems is relative, imprecise, and subject to physical drift. Without synchronized clocks, ordering events across independent nodes requires logical clocks or bounded uncertainty intervals.
theory.whyItMatters: Relying on wall-clock time causes silent data corruption, stale reads, and split-brain states during failovers.
keyMechanisms: Never trust system wall clocks for ordering; use logical clocks or bounded uncertainty.
Vector clocks detect concurrency; they do not resolve conflicts automatically.
Linearizability enforces a strict global real-time ordering visible to all clients.

theory.overview: Replication distributes data redundancy across multiple nodes for fault tolerance. Consensus ensures that a cluster of nodes agrees on state transitions even when individual members crash or networks partition.
theory.whyItMatters: Without majority quorums and consensus, network partitions inevitably cause split-brain data corruption where two nodes accept conflicting writes.
keyMechanisms: Strict majority quorums ((N/2) + 1) prevent split-brain by guaranteeing overlapping nodes.
Raft simplifies Paxos by decomposing consensus into leader election, log replication, and safety.
Fencing tokens protect storage engines against delayed writes from zombie leaders.

keyMechanisms: Consistent hashing bounds key migration to K/N on cluster membership changes.
Virtual nodes homogenize hash space distribution and account for heterogeneous hardware.
Range partitioning enables sequential range scans but creates hot leading-edge write bottlenecks.

keyMechanisms: Cache-aside decouples cache failure from primary database availability.
Singleflight coalescing ensures exactly one request hits the database per key during cache misses.
Probabilistic early refresh (XFetch) eliminates stampedes on hot cache keys.

theory.overview: Distributed locks coordinate access to shared hardware or state across multiple machines. Unlike single-process mutexes, distributed locks operate across unreliable networks and must survive node pauses and clock drift.

keyMechanisms: Distributed locks must use time-bounded leases with active keep-alive renewal.
Storage engines must reject writes with stale fencing tokens.
Consensus-backed locks (etcd/Chubby) are strictly safer than single-node Redis locks.

domainDeepDive.whatIsThisDomain: A distributed system is a collection of autonomous computing nodes that communicate over an unreliable physical network and coordinate their actions by passing messages. Unlike single-node applications operating with shared CPU memory and nanosecond bus latencies, distributed systems must deliver correct, deterministic outcomes across partial node failures, arbitrary packet delays, and unsynchronized physical clocks. The architecture eliminates single points of failure by partitioning and replicating state across fault domains.
domainDeepDive.whyItMatters: Every modern high-scale platform—from payment ledgers and streaming pipelines to distributed databases and globally routed APIs—is fundamentally distributed. Operating at scale means assuming that hardware failure is not an anomaly, but a constant statistical certainty. Mastering this domain transforms an engineer from viewing infrastructure as black-box servers to understanding the exact physical, mathematical, and algorithmic invariants governing data consistency, network partitions, and latency tail percentiles.
domainDeepDive.keyTakeaway: In distributed systems, networks will partition, nodes will crash, and clocks will drift. Never design to prevent failure; design for deterministic fault isolation, bounded blast radiuses, and provable eventual convergence.
coreArchitectureRules: CAP & PACELC Theorem: In the presence of a network partition (P), a system must trade off Consistency (C) for Availability (A). Else (E), when the network is operating normally, the system must trade off Latency (L) for Consistency (C).

The Fallacies of Distributed Computing: Never assume the network is reliable, latency is zero, bandwidth is infinite, the topology is secure, or transport cost is zero. Every remote RPC call is an unreliable network event.

Idempotent State Transitions: In asynchronous networks where packets duplicate and retry indefinitely, every mutating request must carry a unique idempotency key so executing it multiple times produces identical state.

Quorum Intersection Consensus: For strict consistency across N replicas, the read quorum R and write quorum W must satisfy R + W > N. This guarantees at least one node in any read quorum observed the latest write.

Little's Law & Concurrency Limits: Average concurrent requests L equals arrival rate λ multiplied by average latency W (L = λW). As downstream latency spikes, in-flight concurrency explodes, necessitating hard concurrency limits.

failureModes.name: Split-Brain Partition
failureModes.description: A network partition bisects a cluster. Both halves believe the other half is dead, elect independent leaders, and accept conflicting writes simultaneously, causing irreversible data divergence.
failureModes.mitigation: Enforce strict quorum majorities (Q = floor(N/2) + 1) for leader elections and writes. Nodes in the minority partition must immediately step down and reject mutations.

failureModes.name: Cascading Retry Storm (Thundering Herd)
failureModes.description: A temporary database slowdown causes client requests to time out. Clients retry immediately, doubling inbound request volume on an already struggling backend and driving latency to infinity.
failureModes.mitigation: Implement exponential backoff with full jitter and circuit breakers. Drop retries at the edge proxy when downstream failure rates exceed 15%.

failureModes.name: Zombie Node Writes (GC Pause Stale Leader)
failureModes.description: A primary node experiences a 45-second Stop-The-World garbage collection pause. The cluster elects a new leader. When the old leader unpauses, it blindly commits stale writes over the new leader.
failureModes.mitigation: Use monotonically increasing fencing tokens (such as generation IDs or Paxos ballot numbers). Storage nodes reject any write with a token lower than the highest token observed.

failureModes.name: Metastable Failure State
failureModes.description: An incident causes internal queues to saturate. Even after the initial root trigger is resolved, the system remains trapped in a degraded state because recovery traffic continuously exceeds throughput capacity.
failureModes.mitigation: Deploy priority load-shedding, cold-start rate limiters, and fast rejection of non-essential queries to allow the control plane to drain queues before restoring full traffic.

whenToUse: Workloads where data volume or compute capacity exceeds the physical limits of the largest single vertical machine.
Mission-critical systems requiring continuous 99.999% availability that must withstand datacenter and availability zone outages.
Geographically distributed user bases where round-trip latency to a single datacenter exceeds acceptable latency budgets (>150ms).
High-throughput ingestion pipelines (millions of events per second) requiring partitioned, horizontally scalable parallel workers.
whenNotToUse: Early-stage products where operational complexity and network latency overhead outweigh horizontal scaling benefits.
Small engineering teams lacking dedicated SRE, telemetry, and distributed tracing infrastructure.
Workloads requiring absolute ACID serializability across complex relational joins where distributed transactions introduce massive latency penalties.
Applications whose entire active working set fits comfortably within a single modern 128-core, 1TB RAM server.

tradeOffs.pro: Strong linearizability prevents reading stale data and eliminates business logic race conditions.
tradeOffs.con: Incurs cross-node network round-trips for every read/write, increasing p99 latency and sacrificing availability during partitions.

tradeOffs.factor: Synchronous RPC vs Asynchronous Message Queuing
tradeOffs.pro: Synchronous RPC (gRPC/HTTP) is intuitive, easy to debug, and provides immediate confirmation.
tradeOffs.con: Couples services in time and availability, allowing a single slow dependency to exhaust caller thread pools and cause cascading collapse.

tradeOffs.pro: Single-leader architectures simplify conflict resolution and guarantee total write ordering.
tradeOffs.con: The leader is a bottleneck for writes and creates failover fail-stop latency spikes during elections.

productionScenarios.title: Multi-Region Distributed Payment Ledger
productionScenarios.scenario: A global fintech platform processes credit card transactions across EU and US regions. Cross-Atlantic network round-trip is 80ms, but authorization latency SLA is under 200ms.
productionScenarios.outcome: Implemented geographically partitioned accounts with multi-leader conflict-free replicated data types (CRDTs) for non-colliding balance holds, and Raft consensus for finalized end-of-day settlement, achieving 18ms local authorization and zero double-spend anomalies.

productionScenarios.title: Distributed Consistent Hashing Shard Migration
productionScenarios.scenario: A key-value cache cluster of 64 nodes experienced massive cache stampedes and database overloads whenever a single cache node died or scaled out.
productionScenarios.outcome: Deployed consistent hashing with 256 virtual nodes per physical host and bounded-load routing. Adding or removing nodes now only relocates 1/N of keys with zero cluster-wide stampedes.

coreChallenges.title: Network Asynchrony & Packet Loss
coreChallenges.explanation: Ethernet cables, fiber switches, and routers are physical devices prone to congestion, queue bufferbloat, and severed links. Networks delay, drop, duplicate, and reorder packets unpredictably with no guaranteed upper latency bound.

coreChallenges.title: Partial Failures & Undetectable Crashes
coreChallenges.explanation: In a single-process application, a crash terminates everything. In distributed systems, a node can crash or freeze while others continue executing. A sender cannot distinguish between a dead peer, a congested network, or a paused GC process.

coreChallenges.title: Physical Clock Drift & Ordering Ambiguity
coreChallenges.explanation: Quartz crystals on computer motherboards drift by milliseconds every day. Without a trusted global clock, events across nodes cannot be ordered by wall-clock timestamps alone; systems must rely on logical clocks (Lamport, Vector) or atomic synchronized hardware (TrueTime).

coreChallenges.title: The CAP / PACELC Trade-Off Invariant
coreChallenges.explanation: Under network partitions (P), a system must choose between linearizable Consistency (C) and Availability (A). Even under normal non-partitioned operation (E), systems must choose between Latency (L) and Consistency (C).

domainDeepDive.architecturalMindset: Senior distributed systems engineers do not design to prevent failure; they design under the assumption that failure is continuous, unavoidable, and happening right now. They minimize blast radius, isolate fault domains, decouple synchronous dependencies, and engineer for eventual convergence.
